articles.title_orig: China's Trade Strategy Could Reshape Global Agriculture and Input Supply Chains
articles.title_zh: China's Trade Strategy Could Reshape Global Agriculture and Input Supply Chains
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration's effort to reduce China's influence over global trade took a new direction on November 26, following proposed tariffs targeting 14 trading partners. According to an analysis published by Reuters, Washington is encouraging other economies to reassess their commercial and industrial ties with Beijing. For American agriculture, the strategy raises questions about export competitiveness, agricultural input supplies and international investment opportunities , particularly as Latin America expands its role in global food production and agricultural technology.
The proposed measures follow an eight-month investigation by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) into industrial overcapacity. Washington has questioned China's manufacturing practices and the commercial policies of partners including the European Union, Japan and Vietnam. Beijing rejected the allegations, while its economy remains on track to record a trade surplus exceeding $1 trillion for a second consecutive year . Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet in Miami in December, ahead of the January 10, 2027, expiration of their current trade truce.
According to an AgroLatam review of agricultural trade data available as of November 26, the USDA's latest agricultural trade outlook lowered its fiscal 2027 forecast for American agricultural exports to China from $21.5 billion to $20 billion . Although the projection represents a recovery from fiscal 2026, it remains approximately 40% below the value recorded in 2023, reflecting the challenges facing American exporters in an increasingly competitive international market.
Latin America accounts for approximately 14% of global agricultural and fisheries production and 18% of global agrifood exports , according to OECD estimates. Brazil continues to strengthen its position in the Chinese soybean market, with shipments increasing 3.4% year over year between January and September 2026, while purchases from the United States declined 34%. The USDA projects Chinese soybean imports at approximately 4.04 billion bushels for the 2026/27 marketing year.
Beyond Brazil's expanding commodity exports, Argentina is attracting attention for its combination of agricultural production, industrial processing and technological capabilities. According to an AgroLatam review of USDA data, Argentine soybean production is projected to reach approximately 1.93 billion bushels in 2026/27 , while soybean processing is expected to reach its second-highest level on record. Sunflower production is also forecast to establish a new record, supported by international demand for vegetable oils.
Argentina's industrial capacity provides additional opportunities for international agricultural businesses. An October 2026 report from BBVA Research estimates that the country accounts for 45% of global soybean oil exports and 33% of soybean meal exports . The combination of large-scale farming, established research institutions, precision agriculture adoption and competitive processing infrastructure positions Argentina as an attractive market for companies seeking to expand their international operations, particularly in agricultural biotechnology, crop protection and specialized farming technologies.
Elsewhere in the region, Mexico's integration with the American economy supports business opportunities in agricultural machinery, livestock and fresh produce. Colombia combines demand for imported grains with established coffee, avocado and tropical fruit industries. Peru and Chile continue to develop high-value agricultural exports, creating demand for specialized crop protection products, biologicals, irrigation systems and postharvest technologies .
Latin America's high-value crops are driving demand for specialized crop protection, biologicals and advanced farming technologies.
Uruguay and Paraguay maintain important positions in livestock and grain production, while Guatemala and Costa Rica offer specialized markets in coffee, sugarcane and tropical fruit production. These agricultural systems provide opportunities for international manufacturers and technology companies looking to expand their commercial presence across the Americas.
China's importance to agriculture extends beyond commodity purchases. Its chemical industry supplies active ingredients, herbicides, fungicides, insecticides and industrial intermediates used throughout international crop protection supply chains. Changes in trade policies could affect procurement strategies, manufacturing costs and product availability for agricultural businesses.
According to an AgroLatam review of UN Comtrade and World Bank WITS statistics, China exported approximately $9 billion in pesticides and related preparations classified under HS 3808 in 2024 . Brazil received more than $1.9 billion, while direct shipments to the United States exceeded $523 million. Argentina, Paraguay and Peru were also significant customers.
Fertilizer markets also remain exposed to Chinese industrial policies. The OECD's Agricultural Policy Monitoring and Evaluation 2026 report documents Beijing's interventions in nitrogen and phosphate fertilizer trade to prioritize domestic supplies. China's sulfuric acid export ban, introduced in May 2026, adds another consideration for phosphate fertilizer manufacturers and companies sourcing chemical raw materials internationally.
The diversification of agricultural input supply chains could encourage new commercial and research partnerships between American and Latin American companies. Argentina and Brazil have established capabilities in agricultural research, field trials and product development, particularly in biological crop protection, biostimulants, seed technologies and precision agriculture . Argentina's farming systems and technical expertise offer opportunities for international companies to conduct field validation, introduce new formulations and establish regional distribution partnerships, subject to regulatory requirements and commercial conditions.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he pressed Putin in China to pull back 'all military aggression' in Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump says he pressed Putin in China to pull back 'all military aggression' in Europe
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump revealed he asked Vladimir Putin to stop all “military aggression”  in Europe in order to achieve a peace deal with Ukraine.
The president made the request when he met with the Russian president in China last week.
“I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine and made quickly,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday morning of his historic sit down with the Russian leader.
“I really believe this is a strong possibility,” he added.
The statement comes after Trump met with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday night. The two men issued a joint statement urging Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war with Ukraine.
European leaders worry that Putin’s aggression could leave their countries a target for his military.
Great meeting with @POTUS It’s clearer than ever that American leadership remains essential as we build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO https://t.co/1yciLroerD pic.twitter.com/HNHG35akre
Rutte said the alliance is discussing how it would counter such a move.
“These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki,” Rutte told the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin on Monday.
“We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia’s war machine at the moment is running at full speed,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to buy GPUs, sources say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to buy GPUs, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.title_zh: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Fresh US tariffs spark China protest, but unlikely to derail trade talks
articles.title_zh: Fresh US tariffs spark China protest, but unlikely to derail trade talks
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
China warned the US on Thursday that it “reserved the right” to retaliate against Donald Trump ’s latest tariffs, unveiled as the American president remained fixated on his divisive economic policy.
China was one of several Asian economies targeted on Wednesday with a fresh round of levies on certain imports, a major step towards bringing back some of the sweeping global tariffs Mr Trump imposed last year, only to see the US Supreme Court strike them down in February.
China and Vietnam were hit with the steepest proposed tariffs, while Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, India, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, Bangladesh, and Cambodia also faced significant levies. The EU and Switzerland were targeted as well.
China, one of the largest trading partners of the US, faces 20 per cent tariffs over allegations of manufacturing overcapacity. The allegation is that the Asian economic giant is making far more industrial stuff than domestic and global demand can absorb. The levies could rise to as much as 40 per cent for China and 35 percent for Vietnam if Washington determines they aren’t complying with existing trade agreements.
“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” commerce ministry spokesperson He Yadong said, adding that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.
He urged the US to accelerate internal procedures to put a $60 billion tariff reduction arrangement into effect as soon as possible, adding that American and Chinese officials had kept communication over their trade truce.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson accused the US of using claims of industrial overcapacity as a pretext for “political manipulation”.
“The so-called overcapacity is a false proposition and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation,” he said.
“China and the US should work together to implement the important consensus reached between the two heads of state and maintain the momentum of stable development in bilateral economic and trade relations.”
The tariffs were proposed following an investigation led by Mr Trump’s trade negotiator Jamieson Greer into whether foreign trade practices violated existing agreements, or discriminated against American goods.
The fresh round of levies came after the Supreme Court ruled the president’s “Liberation Day” tariffs unlawful in February. The new duties are meant to match the rates agreed upon in trade deals struck since Mr Trump unleashed his trade war.
Under a trade agreement reached earlier this year, China was subject to a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff, in addition to a 10 per cent levy linked to fentanyl. The newly proposed tariff rate of 20 per cent could double if US officials determine that Beijing has failed to honour the terms of the earlier trade truce.
The latest tariff announcement threatened to strain relations between Washington and Beijing barely days after Mr Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping held talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The two leaders are expected to meet again in Miami next month.
The fragile trade truce between Washington and Beijing is set to expire on 10 January. It limits new US tariff increases to 20 percentage points on top of existing levies of 25 percent going back to Mr Trump’s first term. The latest proposal reaches that ceiling.
Under the latest tariff measures, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea face rates of 15 percent.
India faces a tariff of 25 percent, which may be lowered to 17 percent if a trade deal is done. Thailand, Bangladesh, and Cambodia face proposed rates of up to 18 percent. Indonesia and Malaysia are seeking to retain previously agreed rates of 19 percent. Vietnam remains in talks with Washington for a trade deal.

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.content_orig:
Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation.
Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
"The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse said in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy."
The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."
Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.
Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.
The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.
PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from the next day.
Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline."
In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.
The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover.
"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said.
The Norwegian carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war.
India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.
The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.
At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.
Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices."
Correction: This story was updated to reflect that Norse shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attack on Kuwait kills two Italians, Italy’s foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: Iranian attack on Kuwait kills two Italians, Italy’s foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Iranian drones targeted "a vital site" on Thursday, the Kuwait Army said.
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
The two Italian nationals injured in Thursday's Iranian drone attack in Kuwait have died, a spokesperson for Kuwait's Ministry of Defense said in a statement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences to the victim's families in a post on X.
"On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," Meloni said.
The Kuwait Army on Thursday reported that four people were injured by falling shrapnel after an Iranian drone attack targeted "a vital site" in the Gulf state.
The army said in a post to X that Kuwaiti forces "dealt with" the incoming drones. "Material damage also occurred," the statement added.
Those injured were two Italian nationals, one Pakistani national and one Kuwaiti national, the army said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Thursday claimed that two oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz without permission from Tehran "were hit by sea mines" north of the Omani port of Khasab.
The IRGC statement was published by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
Renewed fighting in Yemen's civil war has forced more than 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands over the past week, the United Nations' humanitarian chief said in a statement Wednesday after he arrived in the port city of Aden in the south of the country.
"Fighting, insecurity and heavy restrictions along key supply routes are preventing families from accessing the food and medicine they need to survive," UN Under Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher said, noting that half of Yemen's population needs aid. "Millions are hungry," he added.
Fletcher also called on the Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release our detained UN colleagues and other humanitarians."
"Our work and our people must be protected," he said.
Since 2014, Yemen's internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government -- now based in Aden -- has been fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis, which occupy the capital Sana'a. The conflict has become a widening front in the regional war involving Iran that began in February.

articles.title_orig: China and other U.S. trading partners hit back at Trump’s new tariff plans
articles.title_zh: China and other U.S. trading partners hit back at Trump’s new tariff plans
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

articles.title_orig: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.title_zh: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.content_orig:
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.
Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.
The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.
Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added  to the population in a given year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."
The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.
The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.
The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.
These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.
The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.
Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".
"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."
This is a reference to the so-called "Boris Wave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.
That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.
In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".
Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.
"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."
In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.
As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.
The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via  "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.
As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.
Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".
"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."
Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."
A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

The US maker of Marlboro cigarettes has revealed it is considering making a takeover approach for London-listed JPS and Golden Virginia firm Imperial Brands.
Altria Group, whose companies include Philip Morris USA, said it was also in talks with a third party over a possible offer for part of Imperial Brands, but stressed no agreement on this had been reached.
The US firm, which is headquartered in Richmond , Virginia, said any offer for Imperial Brands would likely be made “solely in cash”.
Imperial Brands shares soared as much as 15% on the news.
The FTSE 100 firm also owns brands including Golden Virginia, Winston and Rizla, as well as smoking alternatives like oral nicotine and its Blu e-cigarette brand.
Imperial is based in Bristol and also has sites in London and Liverpool.
Altria’s bid interest comes after Imperial’s shares have hit multiple-year lows in recent weeks.
Imperial has also been looking to slash costs to boost its performance and, earlier this month, said it was cutting up to 2,500 more jobs globally over the next four years.
This is further to a shake-up which saw it slash about 2,100 roles in the year to September.
The company said, at the time, the transformation was part of a plan to secure at least £320 million in savings by 2030.
Imperial, which employed about 25,800 workers at the end of last year, said it expects to reduce its workforce by between 2,100 and 2,500 by the end of 2030.

articles.title_orig: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing flight delays on Thanksgiving eve
articles.title_zh: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing flight delays on Thanksgiving eve
articles.content_orig:
MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, FLA. (WSVN) - A cargo plane skidded off a runway at Miami International Airport, Wednesday night.
7News cameras captured emergency crews surrounding the FedEx cargo plane that skidded off one of the airport’s runways after overshooting the landing.
As of Thursday morning, the FedEx plane is still sitting in the same spot it landed in.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 originally departed from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis before coming to MIA.
According to an MIA spokesperson, the aircraft overran Runway 26R at around 8:30 p.m., stopping just short of a fence along Northwest 67th Avenue.
Officials said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews responded within 15 minutes.
“Attention all units, attention all units. We have an aircraft that just went off the runway,” an official is heard saying through Broadcastify.
Officials said no injuries were reported, and both people that were inside the cargo plane were seen disembarking and being met by emergency crews.
This outcome was much different from the Sept. 6 incident, in which a 21 Air cargo plane flying for Amazon Prime overshot the runway, crashed down and killed five airport employees while injuring five others.
On Nov. 14, two aircrafts collided on the taxiway at MIA, leaving both planes damaged.
Audio from the control tower on Wednesday’s incident captured the moment officials announced an initial 45-minute ground stop after the FedEx plane ran off the runway.
“The airport is closed. You can cross the runway, cross the runway,” an official is heard saying through Broadcastify.
The closure triggered hourlong delays to departing flights across the board.
On Wednesday night, over 560 flights were delayed and 64 were canceled.
Three out of four runways are operating as of Thursday morning, with FlightAware reporting at least 75 delayed flights and 35 canceled flights.
“It’s kind of terrifying, it’s kind of scary, and I’m just like, ‘What’s happening?’ You know, it’s just really unfortunate when it’s around the holidays that, you know, we’re going to miss this time with our family and stuff,” said a traveler.
Greg Smith told 7News he was trying to get back to London when he found out about the delay.
“We came in, everything was on time for a 10 o’clock departure, we had a little bit to eat, then that’s when we found out everything got diverted to Orlando,” said Smith.
FedEx released a statement Wednesday night, saying
“FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport. We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA.”
MIA officials advise travelers with flights scheduled for Thursday to check in with their airlines for the latest updates on the status of their flights before making their way to the airport, with delays and cancellations expected to continue throughout the day.
The FAA is investigating what led to this incident.

articles.title_orig: The Canadian natural wonder created by a massive meteorite
articles.title_zh: The Canadian natural wonder created by a massive meteorite
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 million years ago, a 5km-wide meteorite smashed into modern-day Quebec. Now, this eerily perfect ring that's visible from space is part of an epic road trip.
Rain pelted my windshield as I steered northwards through the boreal forests of Quebec. Black spruce and balsam firs wove a dense tunnel around the road, and the sky was a low mass of clouds.
Behind me was the windswept coast of the St Lawrence River. Hours ahead lay an unblinking eye that gazes skyward – one so vast it's visible from space. Seen from above, the 72km (45-mile) wide Manicouagan crater forms an eerily perfect ring of water; mountains rise from its centre like a dusky pupil, while rivers and tributaries vein outward from the lake, vanishing deep in the woods.
Manicouagan – AKA: the "Eye of Quebec" – is one of the planet's best-preserved impact craters, created by a 5km- (3-mile-) wide meteorite that threw debris as far as Japan and may have wiped out entire pelagic ecosystems some 214 million years ago. Only when astronauts' photographs from space eventually appeared in 1983 did its vast scope become visible.
Until the 1960s the region surrounding the crater was roadless, but these days, you can drive there on a partially paved rural highway that forms the start of the 1,700km (1,056-mile) Expedition 51 road trip across Quebec and Labrador via the Trans-Labrador Highway, so named for the latitude it follows.
"For Québécois, driving to Manicouagan is the dream," said one local, whom I'd met earlier that summer near the US border. "If you're going, you need two things: a reliable four-wheel-drive truck and clear weather."
This was sensible advice. Yet by the time I filled up my aged and rusting Prius, a huge storm had formed in central Canada and was gaining momentum on an eastbound run. The satellite map showed violent rain showers barrelling directly towards Manicouagan. But it was summer and the eye was calling, so I left my home in Vermont and headed north.
The road to Manicouagan is Quebec Route 389, a two-lane sidewinder that begins in the city of Baie-Comeau on the north shore of the St Lawrence River. To get there I followed the river's coastline north-east 420km (261 miles) from Quebec City, a scenic drive known as the Route des Baleines (Whale Route).
As I drove, I scanned the water for some of the 13 species of cetaceans found in the St Lawrence River during its May-to-October whale-watching season – from slim harbour porpoises to immense blue whales. Standing on the free car ferry across the Saguenay River , I spotted an unmistakable flash of white.
"Belugas!" I cried, pointing to a trio of exuberant, melon-headed whales, which live here year-round – the world's southernmost beluga population .
At Baie-Comeau, I stopped to explore pink-streaked rock formations at Boisé de la Pointe St-Gilles park. Rosy snakes of feldspar wiggled across its waterfront slabs of dark-grey granite, which slope to the river's tidal flat.
The rain started gently as I turned north on Route 389, winding through S-turns to the hydroelectric dam Manic-2. In the summer months, the Hydro-Québec-operated facility – along with the bigger Manic-5, upstream – opens to the public for free guided tours .
Four dams were built on the Manicouagan River in a project that stretched from 1959 to 1970, my guide explained, as we walked through its growling inner workings. When water backed up behind the dams, the Manicouagan impact crater began to fill with water that swirled around the mountainous rise at its centre, creating the "eye" of water that's now visible from space.
"It took nine years for the crater to fill," the guide said, as we discussed the immense earthworks, blasting and engineering the barrages required.
Another 191km (119-mile) drive further to the north, mud-spackled trucks filled the car park at Manic-5, the world's largest multiple-arch-and-buttress dam, whose elegant concrete face seems to defy its massive scope.
I stopped for my second dam tour of the trip. In the surrounding valley, I learned, a temporary city sprang up in the 1960s to house workers, who harnessed the force of entire river systems. In the dam's small museum, I saw images of their families playing in the snow, heading to church, drinking at social halls. The project also brought roads here – including the one that would become Route 389.
"They did many things to build the dams, but what they did not do is ask the Innu first," said Céline Bacon, cultural and tourism officer for the First Nations Innu community of Pessamit, whose traditional territories include those covered by the reservoir.
Best time to visit: Snowmobilers and truckers journey to Manicouagan in the winter, but summer and autumn bring the best road-trip conditions. The Manic-2 and Manic-5 dams are open for tours from mid-June to the end of August.
What to do: Bring your own boat or paddleboard to explore Manicouagan Reservoir. Or, walk one of the trails into the nearby Monts-Groulx mountain range – like the 7km (4.3-mile) round-trip hike to the summit of Mont-Harfang.
Where to stay: Facilities at Manicouagan are limited. Relais-Gabriel at the crater's south-eastern edge offers very basic rooms and meals; the Innu-run Station Uapishka has a shoreline lodge, camping and meals.
The rain turned to a torrent as I continued north; dense stands of boreal forest crowded the edge of the road. For countless generations before the roads were built, Bacon explained, Innu people travelled on foot and by canoe into this landscape, returning each year to seasonal hunting and fishing camps.
"The dams transformed our territory, broke the ways we hunted and fished and gathered," said Bacon, who was raised on family stories of life on the land surrounding Manicouagan. "You can still see some of the old portage routes. My mother talked about them by name."
Rising waters weren't the only rupture. Beginning in the 1950s, Bacon said, the Canadian government increasingly forced Innu families to send their children to government schools, making traditional livelihoods impossible. "With that change, we lost so much of what we knew."
After visiting the dams, many travellers head south back to Baie-Comeau. Others go much farther north, following Route 389 to join the Trans-Labrador Highway to Labrador City.
"We've been planning this for years," said one visitor, from British Columbia, who was bound for the end of the road. He'd waited for retirement before tackling the journey. "When else do you have time for the Trans-Labrador?"
Compared with such trips, my own tempestuous, 11-hour drive from Quebec City to Manicouagan seemed restrained, an epic journey writ small. Yet when I caught my first glimpse of the rain-swollen reservoir, I was thrilled by my final destination.
A passing astronaut would have glimpsed only a thick quilt of fog; around me, saturated evergreens slumped, heavy with rain. I couldn't see much of the crater, but even through the mist the lake – the heart of Unesco's Manicouagan Uapishka Biosphere Reserve – conveyed enormous space and silence.
Scraping grit from boots sodden from that afternoon's hike to nearby Mont-Provencher , I checked into Station Uapishka , a lakeside research station and lodge operated by the Innu of Pessamit and co-founded in partnership with the Unesco reserve. Inside, I met Innu chef Simon Landry-Asselin, who prepares meals at the lodge using ingredients that he forages from the surrounding forest, like spruce tips and the aromatic leaves of Labrador tea, an evergreen shrub.
"This lodge is our chance to share some of who the Innu are with visitors," he explained. "It's my chance to share the ingredients that our ancestors have always known." That night, I dined on baked cod topped with fireweed blossoms Landry-Asselin gathered in the nearby mountains, as wet gusts buffeted the windows.
Yet the next morning, I woke to skies washed clear of clouds. When I walked to the edge of the water, I could see the dark summit of 952m (3,12

articles.title_orig: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.title_zh: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.content_orig:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.title_zh: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.content_orig:
Apple could offer a limited-edition iPhone 20 Pro model that incorporates ceramic, according to the Chinese leaker known as Fixed Focus Digital.
In a post on Weibo , the leaker claimed to have gotten their hands on ceramic components for the 20th-anniversary iPhone, which is expected to launch next year. The leaker said that production capacity for the components is planned to be very low, suggesting they will be for a limited-edition model.
In a follow-up comment, the leaker claimed that the project would enter mass production if it passes engineering validation testing (EVT), and even joked that its scarcity could make it appreciate in value.
The leaker doesn't say what kind of ceramic components they have in their possession, leaving it unclear whether Apple is considering a ceramic rear panel, a larger section of the enclosure, or a smaller exterior part.
Apple already offers ceramic as a premium casing material on the Apple Watch Series 12, which comes in Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic alongside aluminum and titanium options. The company also previously sold ceramic Apple Watch Edition models, including a white ceramic version of the Series 5.
Interestingly, the ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back, and Fixed Focus Digital has previously said next year's iPhone 20 Pro models will use the same glass design , but with more pronounced curves along all four sides of a titanium frame. Ceramic Shield incorporates tiny ceramic crystals within a glass matrix, which preserves transparency while improving durability. However, the wording of the leaker's latest post suggests that ceramic could be applied in a more visually prominent way.
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 with a radical glass-centric redesign featuring a quad-curved display . Leakers have variously referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," but Apple's naming plans remain unclear. The company could well skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to when it introduced the iPhone X in 2017.

articles.title_orig: Huge plume of black smoke seen from space after Houthis claim strike on Saudi’s biggest oil refinery
articles.title_zh: Huge plume of black smoke seen from space after Houthis claim strike on Saudi’s biggest oil refinery
articles.content_orig:
Satellite imagery taken Wednesday showed a huge plume of black smoke rising from Saudi Arabia ’s coastal Ras Tanura peninsula after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed to have attacked the kingdom’s biggest oil refinery.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes “were accurate and direct” and caused a fire at the Ras Tanura facility, part of one of the world’s largest crude oil export terminals.
A shipping source told CNN Thursday that oil loadings at the terminal were suspended after the attack. It’s unclear whether they have resumed.
The Houthis have targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia repeatedly in recent weeks – including an attack on the capital Riyadh’s financial district – as the fallout from the US-Iran war drags on. Riyadh’s international airport was also hit several times last month, killing more than a dozen people.
On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthi rebels said it intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the kingdom’s eastern province. The interception resulted in falling debris, but no injuries were reported, the Coalition Forces spokesman Major General Turki Al-Malki said, citing an initial assessment.
Ras Tanura, which has been targeted previously during the conflict, has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and is part of a broader coastal complex that housed the kingdom’s main export terminal before the US-Iran war began in late February.
CNN has approached Saudi state-owned oil giant Aramco for comment.
Separately on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah port and “destroyed a number of targets” in Saada and Amran governorates, as tit-for-tat strikes between the two sides escalate.
Houthi-affiliated al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi-led forces launched airstrikes on Hodeidah city, including an attack at the Hodeidah International Airport. The port at Hodeidah serves as a key supply route for the Houthis.
Several Saudi airstrikes were reported on Thursday, including on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, according to al-Masirah TV.
CNN has not been able to independently verify the attacks.
Fighting between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July after years of relative calm brought about by a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire. Clashes intensified in recent months after the militant group made an advance toward the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, threatening a new front in the Iran war.
Yemen’s Houthis hold mass funeral as they call for action to protect civilians
In their Wednesday statement, the Houthis also claimed responsibility for a strike on the King Abdullah Economic City in Riyadh that Saudi authorities said wounded 11 people. It was the third such attack this month in the Saudi capital.
In response to the Riyadh attack, the Saudi-led coalition said the “deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects by the Houthi terrorist militia will be met with a firm response.”
An eyewitness in Riyadh told CNN the targeted building, the tallest in the Saudi capital, was the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF). The skyscraper was also struck earlier this month in a missile attack.
CNN’s Tim Lister, Kathleen Magramo, Mohammed Tawfeeq and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Halts Sales to Southeast Asia as U.S. Tightens China Restrictions
articles.content_orig:
Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.
Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.
The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.
Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.
Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes."
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.
U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.
Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says it has intercepted a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says it has intercepted a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, marking a potentially significant development in the country's effort to defend cities from Russia's daily aerial attacks.
The interception was carried out using the Blysk laser air defense system, which was developed and manufactured by Ukrainian defense technology firm Carmine Sky. Technology for laser air defense systems is being developed as part of the wider Private Air Defense program, Zelenskyy's adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov   said in a statement .
About 100 companies across Ukraine have joined the government-backed private air defense initiative.
Russia started deploying jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine earlier this year. The weapons travel faster, making them harder to intercept than the more common propeller-driven attack drones.
In June, Ukraine was only intercepting about 57% of the jet-powered drones , reflecting a significant vulnerability as Ukrainian forces had been shooting down about 90% of the conventional Russian attack drones.
Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.
The laser interception reported by Beskrestnov   this week gives some insight into Ukraine's mounting efforts to adapt both its offenses and defenses as Russia's weapons and tactics evolve.
Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.
Ukraine started testing laser air defense systems over the summer. According to Beskrestnov, the Blysk system was used to protect critical infrastructure, though he declined to give more specifics.
He said a number of Ukrainian companies, including Carmine Sky, are working to develop laser technology, but he cautioned that "it is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser."
"Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he said.

articles.title_orig: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.title_zh: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.content_orig:
Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.
I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).
Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.
I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.
Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).
Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.
Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”
My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.
The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.
Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.
The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.
The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.
I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.
The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.
I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.
Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.
I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.
To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.
My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.
On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.
The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.
Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.
I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.
